The Dutch East Indies were the Dutch possessions in the islands of Southeast Asia, which became Indonesia. Dutch power there began with a trading company in the 1600s and ended with Indonesian independence in 1949.

For two centuries the Dutch East India Company ruled, not the Dutch state. It founded Batavia, now Jakarta, in 1619 and fought for the spice trade, wiping out the people of the Banda Islands for their nutmeg. It held ports and forts more than land. It also set up a supply station at the Cape in 1652, which is why some maps group the Dutch Cape with its Asian holdings.

The company went bankrupt and was dissolved in 1799, and the Dutch state took over in 1800. In the 1800s Dutch rule spread inland:

  • 1825 to 1830: the Java War against Prince Diponegoro.
  • From 1830: the Cultivation System forced Javanese farmers to grow export crops such as coffee and sugar, and paid for much of the Netherlands' budget.
  • 1873 to 1904: the Aceh War in northern Sumatra, one of the longest colonial wars.
  • Early 1900s: control reached its widest, as far as western New Guinea.

Oil, rubber and tin grew in the 1900s, and Royal Dutch Petroleum began here. Educated Indonesians began to imagine one nation across the islands. Japan occupied the colony in 1942. Two days after Japan surrendered in 1945, Sukarno declared independence. The Dutch fought to return, but under American pressure they handed over sovereignty in 1949.
sum: The Dutch East Indies were the Dutch possessions in the islands of Southeast Asia, which became Indonesia. Dutch power there began with a trading company in the 1600s and ended with Indonesian independence in 1949.
